issues.legal_issue: A development scheme may be framed only for an area within the statutory definition of a damaged area, and a declaration made solely under an expired predecessor enactment does not qualify merely because a later enactment contains similar provisions.
material_facts: The scheme was framed under the 1951 Act for an area declared damaged under the 1947 Act, but not declared damaged under either the 1951 Act or the 1949 Act.

The 1949 Act substantially reproduced the 1947 Act, but the 1947 Act was temporary and expired; the Court found no express or implied repeal and re-enactment that would carry the earlier notification forward.
The property sought to be acquired was within the area covered by the scheme.
issues.conclusion: The area did not fall within the definition of a damaged area under the 1951 Act, so the Improvement Trust lacked jurisdiction to frame the scheme and the acquisition proceedings were illegal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(d) of the Punjab Development and Damaged Areas Act, 1951 covers areas notified under that Act or under the Punjab Damaged Areas Act, 1949; it does not cover an area notified only under the 1947 Act. Section 22 of the Punjab General Clauses Act did not carry forward the 1947 notification: there was no repeal and re-enactment, and identical parallel enactments do not establish implied repeal. Although a temporary enactment can be repealed and re-enacted, as recognized in State of Punjab v. Mohar Singh (1956) 1 SCR 893, that did not occur here. Under section 3 of the 1951 Act, the Trust could frame schemes only for damaged areas within the statutory definition.

predicates.development_scheme_proceeding: A public authority frames a development scheme under a law that limits schemes to a defined class of areas.
predicates.area_not_declared_under_current_or_succe: The area was not declared eligible under the governing law or its identified successor law.
predicates.area_declaration_only_under_expired_pred: The only declaration covering the area was made under an expired predecessor enactment.

issues.definition: When a development scheme concerns an area not declared eligible under the governing law or its successor and the only declaration arose under an expired predecessor, the scheme is outside the authority granted by that law.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory provision making publication conclusive evidence that a scheme was duly framed and sanctioned does not prevent a challenge based on the authority’s complete lack of jurisdiction to frame the scheme.
material_facts: The scheme was published after it had been considered and approved by the State Government.
The scheme concerned an area that was outside the statutory definition of a damaged area, so the authorities lacked jurisdiction to frame it.
The affected property owner challenged the scheme and the resulting acquisition proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The publication clause did not bar the challenge because its conclusive effect concerned compliance with procedural formalities, not the existence of jurisdiction; the acquisition proceedings were quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(4) of the Punjab Development and Damaged Areas Act, 1951 makes publication conclusive evidence that a scheme has been duly framed and sanctioned only in relation to the formalities under sections 3, 4 and 5. It does not cure or foreclose a challenge where the authorities had no jurisdiction because the scheme was not for a statutorily eligible area.

predicates.challenge_to_published_development_schem: An affected person challenges a published development scheme and action taken under it.
predicates.scheme_area_outside_authorized_scope: The scheme concerns an area for which the authorities had no statutory authority to frame a scheme.

issues.definition: When an affected person challenges a published development scheme that concerns an area outside the authorities’ statutory scope, publication does not bar the jurisdictional challenge.
